title: Katha traditions
hook: different schools explain Gurbani in different styles

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavishri: Sikh history sung with nothing but the voice. Your line was voice alone. What did you say to someone without a screen in between? Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

The kirtan ends. The music stops, the instruments are set aside, and someone sits down facing the sangat with the scripture open nearby. No singing now. Just talking. They take a single line that was sung a few minutes ago and start to open it: what each word means, which story it brings to mind, what it asks of a person on an ordinary Tuesday. Go to another gurdwara next week and someone else will open the same line in a completely different way. Both are doing katha, explanation. Today is about the different traditions of doing it.
screen: `THE MUSIC STOPS. A VOICE BEGINS.` → `ONE LINE, OPENED UP.` → `NEXT WEEK, A DIFFERENT WAY.`

segments.voice: First, what katha is. The word means telling, or explanation. In a gurdwara, katha is the spoken part beside the sung part: a giani, a learned explainer, takes Gurbani and opens it for the sangat. Second, the styles. Some explainers go word by word, slowly, giving the meaning of each term and how it fits the grammar of the line. Some tell sakhis, stories from the lives of the Gurus, and let the story carry the meaning. Some draw on the vocabulary of older Indian philosophy, as the Nirmala and Udasi scholars did. Some trace their way of reading back through a teaching lineage; the Damdami Taksal, for one, says its line of teachers goes back to Guru Gobind Singh. And some speakers today explain with history, science, or everyday life, for listeners who grew up far from Punjab. Third, why there are many ways. In the sixteenth pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: if anyone tries to tell of it and reflect on it, there is no counting what the Creator has made. If the subject is that wide, no single explanation can finish it. Each school is holding up a lamp to one part of a very large room. Fourth, how Sikhs hold the differences. Explainers sometimes disagree, and Sikhs argue about which readings are faithful, and that argument is part of a living tradition. What sits above all of them is the Guru Granth Sahib itself. The katha is a servant of the line, never its replacement. Many ways to explain, one line being explained.
screen: `KATHA: THE SPOKEN EXPLANATION.` · `WORD BY WORD, STORY, OR LINEAGE.` · `THERE IS NO COUNTING IT.` · `THE LINE SITS ABOVE THEM ALL.` · then, large: `MANY WAYS TO EXPLAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: compare two explanations. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one line of scripture you know, from any book that matters to you. Recall two ways you've heard it explained, or two ways it could be read. Don't choose between them yet. Hold the first, and see what it lights up. Then hold the second, and see what it lights up. Then let the line itself sit in the middle, bigger than both. The bell holds the time.
Katha traditions. The schools and styles of explaining Gurbani aloud: word by word, through stories, through teaching lineages, through everyday life. Today's word.

Your line: many ways to explain. Today, when someone explains something you thought you already understood, let them finish, and keep one new thing they showed you. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras a giani may give katha after kirtan, explaining a line or hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib; explainers from different schools use word-by-word meaning, stories of the Gurus, or present-day examples.

fork.setup: you hear the same line explained two different ways in two weeks. what do you do?
options: decide one explainer is wrong and stop listening.
hold both and ask what each lets you see.
stop listening to explanations at all.
fork.reveal: Sikhs do argue about faithful readings, but the line sits above all the explainers. in paraphrase, Japji says there's no counting what the Creator has made.
